# Lynn Conway – Summary
Lynn Conway was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer whose most significant contributions were in the development of very-large-scale integration (VLSI) technology. After completing her education with B.S. and M.S.E.E. degrees at Columbia University, Conway began her career at IBM Research, where she co-invented out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, a foundational concept in superscalar computer design. After her gender transition in 1968 led to her dismissal from IBM (an action for which IBM publicly apologized and granted her a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020), Conway rebuilt her career and went on to play a critical role at Memorex, Xerox PARC, DARPA, and the University of Michigan.
Conway's co-invention, alongside Carver Mead, of scalable VLSI design methodologies and the MOSIS rapid prototyping infrastructure revolutionized chip design and manufacturing, fostering the rise of the electronic design automation industry and the foundry model. Their textbook, *Introduction to VLSI Systems* , became the standard for university-level chip design education, catalyzing innovation throughout the technology industry. Conway received many honors, including election to the National Academy of Engineering and the IEEE Fellow distinction. She was also recognized for her activism in transgender rights, providing resources and advocating for equal opportunities in STEM, and was listed among influential transgender people by Time Magazine. Conway passed away on June 9, 2024, at the age of 86.
